sections.title: Human Dignity
sections.body: We hold that human dignity is unconditional. It cannot be earned or lost, granted or revoked. You have it because you are human — wherever you were born, whatever you have done, whoever you are. This is the foundation everything else rests on.
sections.rationale: Human dignity is stated first because it is the premise every other principle depends on. Without it, the economic and governance structures that follow have no moral foundation.

sections.title: Self-Governance
sections.body: We govern ourselves through genuine deliberation. No authority is legitimate here that does not flow from the genuine consent of the people subject to it. We trust ordinary people to make good decisions — not ideology, not party, not wealth.
sections.rationale: Self-governance is stated as a structural principle, not a preference. Institutions that derive authority from something other than the consent of the governed are not legitimate institutions of this society.

sections.title: Honest Inquiry
sections.body: We believe in honest inquiry. The world is what it is regardless of what we wish it to be. We commit to following evidence wherever it leads.
sections.rationale: Communities that cannot update their beliefs in response to evidence cannot solve real problems. Honest inquiry is an operational requirement, not a philosophical position.

sections.title: Mutual Obligation
sections.body: We accept collective responsibility for every member's food, care, and security. Mutual obligation, not charity.
sections.rationale: The distinction between mutual obligation and charity matters. Charity is voluntary and conditional; mutual obligation is built into membership. Members have a right to this support, not merely a hope for it.

sections.title: Economic Sovereignty
sections.body: Economic sovereignty belongs to the people who live and work in a community. We reject systematic exploitation in all its forms.
sections.rationale: Economic sovereignty is the capacity to make collective decisions about production, distribution, and exchange without external coercion. A community that cannot control its economic life cannot fulfill its obligations to its members.

sections.title: Building Our Own
sections.body: We build our own institutions rather than waiting for failing ones. We are practitioners first — we measure success not by what we believe but by what our community can do.
sections.rationale: The Society is defined by what it builds, not what it believes. This principle guards against the community becoming a discussion group rather than a functional institution.

sections.title: Stewardship
sections.body: We are stewards of the natural world. We treat land, water, and living systems as held in trust for those who come after us.
sections.rationale: The community's obligations extend beyond its current members to future members and to the natural systems that make human life possible.

sections.title: Common Purpose
sections.body: We protect our capacity to think and decide for ourselves. We build community life that restores genuine connection and common purpose.
sections.rationale: Communities that cannot deliberate together cannot govern themselves. Common purpose is not assumed — it is built through shared institutions and shared life.

sections.title: Accountability
sections.body: We hold ourselves to genuine accountability — to each other, to our principles, and to all people.
sections.rationale: Accountability without consequence is not accountability. This principle applies to every member and every institution of the Society.

sections.title: Human Decency
sections.body: We hold ourselves to basic human decency. How we treat each other is not separate from what we are building — it is what we are building.
sections.rationale: The manner of the community's internal life is not distinct from its purpose. A community that builds just institutions through unjust means has not built what it intended.

sections.title: Service
sections.body: We hold that positions of leadership and governance exist solely to serve the people subject to them. Leadership is a burden accepted, not a privilege claimed. Anyone who seeks governance authority for personal gain, status, or power is unfit to hold it.
sections.rationale: This principle defines the orientation required of those who hold governance roles. It is enforced institutionally through sortition — random selection removes the incentive to seek power.

sections.title: The Limits of Markets
sections.body: We acknowledge that markets are ill-suited to providing certain categories of goods — in particular those where human need is too urgent to permit the discipline of price, those where the profit motive is directly opposed to the purpose of the service, and those where the full cost of provision or the full value of preservation cannot be captured in a transaction between buyer and seller.
sections.rationale: This principle does not reject markets generally. It names the specific conditions under which market provision fails and community provision is required.

sections.title: Liberty
sections.body: The liberty of all people is sacred. The Society explicitly rejects incarceration as a response to poverty, addiction, mental illness, or social conditions the Society itself is obligated to address.
sections.rationale: Liberty is not merely freedom from external interference — it requires that the community not use its own institutional power to confine people for problems it has an obligation to address through care rather than punishment.

sections.title: Community Authority
sections.body: All authority originates with and belongs to the community in its entirety. A Ben Franklin Society must maintain this principle in its institutional design — not as a statement of belief but as an operational reality. Authority is delegated downward for practical purposes and is always recallable upward. The community has final say over all institutions, bodies, and decisions within the Society.
sections.rationale: This minimum ensures that the governance structures required by the rest of this section cannot be turned against the community that created them.

sections.title: General Assembly
sections.body: A Ben Franklin Society must maintain a General Assembly drawn by sortition from the eligible adult membership. The General Assembly is the primary legislative body of the Society, acting by delegation from the community. It must be genuinely sortition-drawn — no elections, no appointments, no hereditary positions. The randomness of selection is not a procedural detail. It is the mechanism by which the General Assembly remains the community's body rather than any faction's instrument.
sections.rationale: A sortition-drawn assembly cannot be captured by organized interest groups because there is no election to win.

sections.title: The Frank
sections.body: A Ben Franklin Society must issue and maintain the Frank as its community currency. The Frank is issued on the basis of the person-year — equal for every member — and flows through the Treasury into the community's common life. The Frank is the material expression of the community's economic sovereignty.
sections.rationale: A community that does not control its own currency has not achieved the economic sovereignty Principle V requires.

sections.title: Financial Infrastructure
sections.body: A Ben Franklin Society must maintain the foundational financial institutions without which a Frank economy cannot function: a Central Bank responsible for Frank issuance and the membership roll; a Community Bank maintaining the ledger of Frank holdings and transactions; a Treasury receiving dues and disbursing funds per General Assembly appropriation; and a Social Insurance Fund providing regular support to elderly and disabled members.
sections.rationale: These four institutions are not optional. They are the infrastructure of economic self-governance.

sections.title: The Colleges
sections.body: A Ben Franklin Society must maintain the Colleges framework — the system of peer bodies through which the community acknowledges domain expertise and draws qualified practitioners for governance in specialized domains. The specific Colleges a society maintains will vary with its size, population, and development. The framework itself — peer credentialing, qualified sortition, General Assembly creation and accountability — must be maintained.
sections.rationale: The Colleges prevent both unqualified populism and expert technocracy. Domain decisions are made by people the community has recognized as qualified practitioners.

sections.title: Food Security
sections.body: A Ben Franklin Society must treat food security as a community obligation. No member shall go without adequate nutrition through failure of the community to act. The Society must maintain the institutional capacity to ensure this — through food services, food reserves, and agricultural capacity development.
sections.rationale: Food security is listed first among the service obligations because it is the most basic. A community that cannot feed its members has not begun to fulfill its purpose.

sections.title: Healthcare
sections.body: A Ben Franklin Society must treat healthcare as a right of membership. The Society must maintain health services at whatever level of capacity it can sustain, working continuously to expand that capacity. No member shall be without access to the best healthcare the community can provide.
sections.rationale: Healthcare is a right of membership, not a market good. The obligation is to provide the best the community can manage — and to keep working to expand that capacity.

sections.title: Shelter
sections.body: A Ben Franklin Society must guarantee that no member is without adequate shelter through failure of the community to act. The Society must maintain the institutional capacity to fulfill this guarantee — through housing services, emergency shelter, and maintenance support.
sections.rationale: Shelter, like food and healthcare, is a human necessity whose guarantee is a charter requirement.

sections.title: Human Dignity in Practice
sections.body: A Ben Franklin Society must maintain institutional protections for human dignity that give Principle I operational force. No member shall be removed from membership, deprived of their rights, or subjected to institutional action without due process. No institution of the Society shall treat any member as less than fully human.
sections.rationale: The unconditional dignity of Principle I is not merely a statement of belief — it is a constitutional constraint on every institution the Society maintains.

sections.title: Fair Dealing with Neighboring Societies
sections.body: A Ben Franklin Society must deal fairly with other member societies. A Ben Franklin Society may not use control of essential resources — water, land access, transport routes, food supply, or infrastructure — to coerce, extract from, or systematically disadvantage another society. Trade and mutual aid between societies must be conducted in good faith.
sections.rationale: The economic sovereignty guaranteed to members within a society extends, in principle, to the relations between societies. A society that leverages necessity into exploitation has violated the same principle it claims to uphold for its own members.

sections.title: Held in Common
sections.body: This Charter is held collectively by all Ben Franklin Societies. It is not the property of any single society, any founding body, or any individual. It belongs to the network of communities that have adopted it and committed to living by it. No single society may amend it. Changes to the Charter require the deliberate consensus of the societies that hold it.
sections.rationale: The Charter's authority derives from its being held in common. A charter that any single society could amend would not be a shared standard — it would be a local document.

sections.title: A Definition, Not a Constitution
sections.body: This Charter defines what a Ben Franklin Society is. It does not govern how any particular society governs itself. Each society maintains its own constitution — its own foundational document establishing the specific institutions, processes, and commitments by which it lives the Charter's principles and maintains the Charter's institutional minimums. A society's constitution may go further than this Charter requires. It may not fall short of it.
sections.rationale: The Charter sets a floor, not a ceiling. Individual societies have latitude in how they organize themselves, provided they maintain the institutional minimums and honor the founding principles.

sections.title: A Living Standard
sections.body: The Charter is a living standard — a definition that communities are measured against, not just at founding but continuously. A Ben Franklin Society that abandons its General Assembly, that surrenders its Frank, that allows its members to go without food or shelter or care, has ceased to be a Ben Franklin Society in any meaningful sense.
sections.rationale: Founding commitments do not exempt a community from ongoing accountability. The Charter names what we are. Living up to it is the ongoing work.
